title: Job 2 — The second council scene and the second test

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֔וֹם וַיָּבֹ֙אוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים לְהִתְיַצֵּ֖ב עַל־יְהוָ֑ה וַיָּב֤וֹא גַֽם־הַשָּׂטָן֙ בְּתֹכָ֔ם לְהִתְיַצֵּ֖ב עַל־יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: The day came when the sons of the Elohim came to present themselves before YHWH — and the adversary also came among them to present himself before YHWH.

notes.official: **The second council scene opens.** The verse is **nearly identical** to 1:6 — same opening formula (*vay'hi ha-yom*), same convocation (*bnei ha-elohim... l'hityatzev al-YHWH*), same arrival (*va-yavo gam ha-satan b'tokham*). The chapter is staging the council as a **periodic recurrence** — these gatherings happen *on the day*, repeatedly. // One small addition: 2:1 adds *l'hityatzev al-YHWH* to ha-satan's arrival as well — making explicit that ha-satan presents himself in the same posture as the rest of the bnei ha-elohim. The chapter is reinforcing the role-internal-to-council framing of chapter 1.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־הַשָּׂטָ֔ן אֵ֥י מִזֶּ֖ה תָּבֹ֑א וַיַּ֨עַן הַשָּׂטָ֤ן אֶת־יְהוָה֙ וַיֹּאמַ֔ר מִשֻּׁ֣ט בָּאָ֔רֶץ וּמֵהִתְהַלֵּ֖ךְ בָּֽהּ׃

i18n.en: YHWH said to the adversary, "From where do you come?" And the adversary answered YHWH and said, "From roaming the earth and walking back and forth on it."

notes.official: **The same opening exchange.** YHWH's question and ha-satan's response are nearly verbatim from 1:7. The chapter is staging the council as a **repeatable scene** — the same opening protocol, the same response. The narrative is signaling that ha-satan's range-the-earth-and-report function is its standing-role, not a one-time investigation.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֜ה אֶל־הַשָּׂטָ֗ן הֲשַׂ֣מְתָּ לִבְּךָ֮ אֶל־עַבְדִּ֣י אִיּוֹב֒ כִּי֩ אֵ֨ין כָּמֹ֤הוּ בָּאָ֙רֶץ֙ אִ֣ישׁ תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר יְרֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְסָ֣ר מֵרָ֑ע וְעֹדֶ֙נּוּ֙ מַחֲזִ֣יק בְּתֻמָּת֔וֹ וַתְּסִיתֵ֥נִי ב֖וֹ לְבַלְּע֥וֹ חִנָּֽם׃

i18n.en: YHWH said to the adversary, "Have you set your heart on my servant Job? For there is none like him on the earth — a man blameless and upright, one who fears Elohim and turns from evil. He still holds firm to his integrity, and you incited me against him to swallow him without cause."

notes.official: **The verdict on round one — and the term 'incited'.** YHWH reaffirms Job's characterization (the same five-fold formula from 1:1 and 1:8), then notes the persistence: *odennu machaziq b'tumato* — *he still holds firm to his integrity*. *Tumah* is the noun-form of *tam* — *integrity, completeness*. Job has maintained his *tom-v-yashar* status through the first test. // *Va-tesiteni vo l'val'o chinnam* — *and you incited me against him to swallow him without cause*. Two notable verbs. // First, *vatesiteni* — *you incited me* — from the verb *sut* (incite, instigate, provoke). The verb is also used of the lying spirit in 1 Kgs 22:20-22 (incite Ahab) and of Saul's persecution of David (1 Sam 26:19). YHWH is acknowledging that the test was **at ha-satan's initiative** — YHWH was *prompted* into it. The chapter is staging the divine response as *responding* to ha-satan's challenge rather than originating it. // Second, *chinnam* (the same word as 1:9) — *without cause / for nothing*. The chapter is doing wordplay: ha-satan accused Job of being righteous *chinnam* (without compensation, transactional); YHWH now describes the test as having been undertaken *chinnam* (without cause, gratuitously). The accusation has been reversed: the *adversary* is the one who acted without cause. // The verb *l'val'o* (to swallow him) is the strongest possible language for total destruction. YHWH is naming the test as *l'val'o* — a swallowing-up — which makes the first test's escalation explicit.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֧עַן הַשָּׂטָ֛ן אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה וַיֹּאמַ֑ר ע֣וֹר בְּעַד־ע֗וֹר וְכֹל֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לָאִ֔ישׁ יִתֵּ֖ן בְּעַ֥ד נַפְשֽׁוֹ׃

i18n.en: The adversary answered YHWH and said, "Skin for skin — all that a person has, he will give for his life."

notes.official: **The adversary's second argument: *skin for skin*.** ***Or be'ad or*** is a proverb-form. The Hebrew preposition *be'ad* (for, on behalf of, in exchange for) sets up an exchange-relationship. Two readings have circulated: // (1) **Self-preservation reading.** Skin (Job's body) is what he'll give in exchange for his life — i.e., he'll sacrifice anything *up to* his own bodily integrity to preserve his life. The argument: Job has weathered the loss of family and property, but he hasn't yet had to give up *himself*. // (2) **Substitution reading.** One sheds the skin of others (his children, his servants) to save one's own skin — i.e., Job tolerated the first test because the losses were external; he'll break when the test reaches his own body. // Both readings converge on the same prediction: the next test must reach Job's body. The chapter's argument-structure is escalating from *what Job has* to *what Job is*. // The proverb *or be'ad or* has not been securely identified in any other ANE source. The construction is unique in the Hebrew Bible. The chapter is staging the adversary as using folk-wisdom that the audience would recognize.

paragraphs.text: אוּלָם֙ שְֽׁלַֽח־נָ֣א יָֽדְךָ֔ וְגַ֥ע אֶל־עַצְמ֖וֹ וְאֶל־בְּשָׂר֑וֹ אִם־לֹ֥א אֶל־פָּנֶ֖יךָ יְבָרֲכֶֽךָּ׃

i18n.en: But put out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh — and surely he will curse you to your face.

notes.official: **The proposed second test.** The adversary's prediction is identical to 1:11 in its closing formula (*al-panekha y'varakhekka* — *to your face he will curse you*, using *barakh* as euphemism for curse — see commentary at 1:5). // The proposed test-action: *ga el atzmo v'el b'saro* — *touch his bone and his flesh*. The chapter is specifying the **bodily** test, where Job himself becomes the target. *Etzem* (bone) and *basar* (flesh) are the same vocabulary cluster as Ezekiel 37's staged-construction sequence (gidim → basar → `or → ruach); here they are the dimensions of Job's bodily integrity to be reached.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר יְהוָ֛ה אֶל־הַשָּׂטָ֖ן הִנּ֣וֹ בְיָדֶ֑ךָ אַ֖ךְ אֶת־נַפְשׁ֥וֹ שְׁמֹֽר׃

i18n.en: YHWH said to the adversary, "Behold, he is in your hand — only spare his life."

notes.official: **The second permission and its new limit.** *Hinno b'yadkha* — *behold, he is in your hand*. The limit is moved: in 1:12 the limit was *Job himself*; now Job himself is included, with only *nafsho* (his life-soul, his life-as-such) excluded. The escalation is precise — what was protected becomes available, what remains protected becomes the irreducible. // *Et nafsho shmor* — *only spare his life*. The verb *shamar* (guard, watch over, preserve) makes ha-satan responsible for **not killing Job**. The boundary is: Job's bodily integrity may be attacked, his life must be preserved.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּצֵא֙ הַשָּׂטָ֔ן מֵאֵ֖ת פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וַיַּ֤ךְ אֶת־אִיּוֹב֙ בִּשְׁחִ֣ין רָ֔ע מִכַּ֥ף רַגְל֖וֹ ועד [וְעַ֥ד] קָדְקֳדֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: The adversary went out from before YHWH and struck Job with severe sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.

notes.official: **The bodily affliction.** *Shechin ra* — *severe sores* — describes a comprehensive skin-disease covering Job from sole to scalp. *Shechin* (שְׁחִין) is the Hebrew Bible's standard term for severe inflammatory skin afflictions; it appears at Ex 9:9-11 (the sixth Egyptian plague), Lev 13:18-23 (Levitical priestly diagnosis of skin disease), Deut 28:27, 35, 2 Kgs 20:7 (Hezekiah's affliction). The exact dermatological identification is debated (smallpox, severe boils, leprosy in the old sense, an infected eruption); the chapter does not specify the medical-diagnostic detail. // *Mi-kaf raglo v'ad qodqodo* — *from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head* — the standard Hebrew Bible totality-formula (cf. Deut 28:35, 2 Sam 14:25, Isa 1:6) — the affliction is bodily-comprehensive. // *Ketiv/qere note*: *v'ad* (qere) for *u'ad* (ketiv) — minor preposition variant; the qere reading is adopted.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּֽקַּֽח־ל֣וֹ חֶ֔רֶשׂ לְהִתְגָּרֵ֖ד בּ֑וֹ וְה֖וּא יֹשֵׁ֥ב בְּתוֹךְ־הָאֵֽפֶר׃

i18n.en: He took a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat in the midst of the ashes.

notes.official: **Two iconic details.** *Cheres l'hithgared bo* — *a potsherd to scrape himself with*. The verb *garad* (scrape, scratch) names the action; *cheres* is a broken pottery shard. The image is one of the Hebrew Bible's most-cited iconographies: the suffering-figure scraping his sores with a piece of broken pottery. // *V'hu yoshev b'tokh ha-efer* — *and he sat in the midst of the ashes*. *Efer* (ashes, dust) is the standard Hebrew Bible substance of mourning (cf. Esth 4:1, 4:3 of Mordecai; Jer 6:26 of mourning generally; Job 42:6 of Job's eventual self-abasement). The chapter is establishing the mourning-posture: stripped of property, family, and now bodily integrity, Job sits in ashes scraping at his afflicted skin. // Both details — the potsherd and the ashes — become the iconographic signature of Job in art and exegesis. The chapter is staging the lowest possible posture for a wealthy patriarch.

paragraphs.text: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ אִשְׁתּ֔וֹ עֹדְךָ֖ מַחֲזִ֣יק בְּתֻמָּתֶ֑ךָ בָּרֵ֥ךְ אֱלֹהִ֖ים וָמֻֽת׃

i18n.en: His wife said to him, "Are you still holding firm to your integrity? Curse Elohim — and die."

notes.official: **The wife's challenge.** *Odekha machaziq b'tumatekha* — *are you still holding firm to your integrity?* The wife is using the **same verb** YHWH used in 2:3 (*odennu machaziq b'tumato* — *he still holds firm to his integrity*). The chapter is staging her as having direct insight into the divine assessment — though she draws the opposite conclusion. // *Barekh Elohim va-mut* — literally *bless Elohim and die*, but *barekh* is again the **euphemism for curse** (the third occurrence of this scribal device in the book: cf. 1:5, 1:11, 2:5; commentary at 1:5 for the euphemism). The wife's plain instruction: *curse Elohim and die*. // The wife has been read at every level — as faithless tempter (the patristic reading), as compassionate-deliverer (suggesting Job blaspheme to provoke YHWH's killing-blow as merciful release), or as authentic dissent (her position registers a legitimate response to the apparent injustice). The chapter does not editorialize; Job's response in v10 sets the verdict the chapter wants — but it does not condemn the wife as such.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלֶ֗יהָ כְּדַבֵּ֞ר אַחַ֤ת הַנְּבָלוֹת֙ תְּדַבֵּ֔רִי גַּ֣ם אֶת־הַטּ֗וֹב נְקַבֵּל֙ מֵאֵ֣ת הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים וְאֶת־הָרָ֖ע לֹ֣א נְקַבֵּ֑ל בְּכָל־זֹ֛את לֹא־חָטָ֥א אִיּ֖וֹב בִּשְׂפָתָֽיו׃

i18n.en: He said to her, "You are speaking as one of the foolish women speaks. Should we accept good from the Elohim and not accept bad?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

notes.official: **Job's second response.** ***Gam et ha-tov n'qabel me-et ha-Elohim v'et ha-ra lo n'qabel*** — *should we accept the good from the Elohim and not accept the bad?* The question is rhetorical: the symmetry of acceptance is required by the relationship. If you accept the good as coming from a single source, you accept the bad as coming from the same source. // The verbal pair *tov v-ra* (good and bad) is the same vocabulary as Gen 2:9, 2:17 (the tree of *da'at tov v-ra* — *knowing good and bad*) and Gen 3:5, 3:22 (the human became like the Elohim knowing good and bad). The chapter is invoking the Edenic-vocabulary cluster: humans know good and bad. The capacity to *know good and bad* (acquired in Gen 3) is here applied — Job *knows* both, and accepts both. // The verb *n'qabel* (we shall accept, from *qibel* — receive, accept) is the chapter's standing-claim verb. Job is not endorsing the bad; he is accepting it as coming from the same source as the good. The chapter is making a sophisticated theological-philosophical move: the categorial unity of good and bad in the divine economy. // *B'khol-zot lo chata Iyov bisefatav* — *In all this Job did not sin with his lips*. The narrator's verdict closes the second test, slightly modified from 1:22 (which closed *lo chata Iyov v'lo natan tiflah l'Elohim* — *Job did not sin nor charged Elohim with anything unseemly*). The 2:10 verdict adds *bisefatav* — *with his lips* — a slight narrowing that has been read as the chapter leaving room for what Job will eventually do *with his thoughts* in the later dialogues. The narrowing is subtle but textually present.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיִּשְׁמְע֞וּ שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת ׀ רֵעֵ֣י אִיּ֗וֹב אֵ֣ת כָּל־הָרָעָ֣ה הַזֹּאת֮ הַבָּ֣אָה עָלָיו֒ וַיָּבֹ֙אוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ מִמְּקֹמ֔וֹ אֱלִיפַ֤ז הַתֵּימָנִי֙ וּבִלְדַּ֣ד הַשּׁוּחִ֔י וְצוֹפַ֖ר הַנַּעֲמָתִ֑י וַיִּוָּעֲד֣וּ יַחְדָּ֔ו לָב֥וֹא לָנֽוּד־ל֖וֹ וּלְנַחֲמֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: When the three companions of Job heard of all this evil that had come upon him, each of them came from his place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite — and they made an appointment together to come to console him and to comfort him.

notes.official: **The three friends arrive.** *Elifaz ha-Temani* — *Eliphaz the Temanite* — Teman is a region in Edom (the southern Transjordan), associated with wisdom-tradition (Jer 49:7). *Bildad ha-Shuchi* — *Bildad the Shuhite* — Shuah is one of Abraham's sons by Keturah (Gen 25:2), associated with the Aramean periphery. *Tzofar ha-Na'amati* — *Zophar the Naamathite* — Naamah is uncertain; possibly an Edomite-Aramean location. // All three are **non-Israelite peripheral-Aramean Wisdom figures**. The chapter is staging the dialogue that follows as **Wisdom-tradition discourse** among Aramean periphery sages — the same cultural register as Job himself (Job of Uz, also non-Israelite). The book is positioning itself in the international Wisdom-literature tradition of the ANE (Sumerian / Akkadian / Egyptian / Edomite Wisdom traditions; cognate with the *Babylonian Theodicy* and the *Dialogue of Pessimism*).

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׂא֨וּ אֶת־עֵינֵיהֶ֤ם מֵרָחוֹק֙ וְלֹ֣א הִכִּירֻ֔הוּ וַיִּשְׂא֥וּ קוֹלָ֖ם וַיִּבְכּ֑וּ וַיִּקְרְעוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ מְעִל֔וֹ וַיִּזְרְק֥וּ עָפָ֛ר עַל־רָאשֵׁיהֶ֖ם הַשָּׁמָֽיְמָה׃

i18n.en: When they raised their eyes from afar, they did not recognize him. They raised their voices and wept; each tore his robe and threw dust upon his head, skyward.

notes.official: **Three mourning rites.** The friends do not recognize Job at first (the affliction has disfigured him beyond recognition). They then perform three mourning rites: *yisu qolam va-yivku* (raised their voices and wept), *yiqra'u ish me'ilo* (each tore his robe — the same rite Job performed at 1:20), *yizr'qu afar al-rashehem ha-shamaymah* (threw dust upon their heads, skyward). // The dust-throwing-skyward is iconographic Hebrew Bible mourning-imagery (cf. Lam 2:10, Josh 7:6, 1 Sam 4:12, Neh 9:1). The verbal direction *ha-shamaymah* (skyward) is unusual — the friends throw the dust *upward*, where it falls back down on them. The action is comprehensive: they place themselves in the same mourning-posture Job is already in.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּשְׁב֤וּ אִתּוֹ֙ לָאָ֔רֶץ שִׁבְעַ֥ת יָמִ֖ים וְשִׁבְעַ֣ת לֵיל֑וֹת וְאֵין־דֹּבֵ֤ר אֵלָיו֙ דָּבָ֔ר כִּ֣י רָא֔וּ כִּֽי־גָדַ֥ל הַכְּאֵ֖ב מְאֹֽד׃

i18n.en: They sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word to him, for they saw that his pain was very great.

notes.official: **Seven days of silent presence.** *Shivat yamim v'shivat leilot* — *seven days and seven nights*. The number seven is the Hebrew Bible's mourning-week canonical duration (cf. Gen 50:10 of Joseph mourning for Jacob, 1 Sam 31:13 / 1 Chr 10:12 of mourning for Saul, Sir 22:12 of seven-day mourning for the dead). The chapter is staging the friends as observing the full mourning-week before any conversation begins. // *Ein dover elav davar* — *none spoke a word to him*. The silence is total. The chapter ends on this seven-day silent presence — the dialogue that begins in chapter 3 will open with Job himself speaking first (*va-yiftach Iyov et pihu va-y'qalel et yomo* — *Job opened his mouth and cursed his day*, 3:1). The narrative arc closes here: the prologue's wager has been laid (chapters 1-2), the test has been delivered, Job has held firm, the friends have arrived in solidarity, the silence has begun. // The dialogue-prologue is complete. The dialogue-proper (chapters 3-31), the Elihu speeches (32-37), and the divine speeches (38-42) will follow. This is the book's narrative-framing prologue.
